translation: The winter of 1993 was most significant to me because my father came back, just a week before my mother got married.
One afternoon in December, he came to look for me at school.
I ran all the way to the gate and saw him from a distance, past the iron bars, smoking outside.
He was wearing a black trench coat with his collar turned up covering half his face.
Somehow, even without seeing him clearly, I could tell that he seemed quite distressed.
My heart sank and tears welled up in my eyes.
I never thought that my mother would consider remarrying.
Perhaps subconsciously, I believed she should continue to suffer because of my dad's departure, just like me.
Besides, I felt as if she lacked the capacity to find happiness.
The truth might have indeed been this way, yet happiness had the ability to find her.
Isn't it so?
For a beautiful woman like her who didn't have to lift a finger; all she needed was to stand still where she was.
I still remember that the winter of that year was especially long, half past April and the spring flowers had not yet bloomed.
My parents' divorce made you very depressed.
We hadn't had any new games in a long time, and as twilight fell, we would sit listlessly on the rooftop of the necropolis tower.
Among the scattered body parts in the yard, a few more arms were added.
We used hooks to pull them together, forming a statue of Guanyin with many hands and eyes.
Actually, my father knew nothing about business and simply went to seek assistance from a cousin he wasn't very close with.
My grandmother had a younger sister who moved to Beijing years ago, where she got married and had children.
This cousin was her eldest son, and within our whole family, he was always seen as an odd one out.
Just now, you mentioned that every person has a time of fate when life seems to have suddenly been reined in.
Mine should be at the age of eight.
That autumn, my father left Jinan and went to Beijing alone.
From then on, I no longer had a home.
I had no intention of honoring the meeting.
No matter the reason, I felt there was no necessity for us to meet again.
I sat on the sofa, chain-smoking as dusk fell.
Suddenly, there was a knock at the door.
The water delivery boy stood at the doorway with a large bucket, saying he had come to deliver water to a house in the western suburb.
He was wearing a dirty grey woolen hat and looked absent-minded.
Our conversation was arduous.
Each moment of silence felt so oppressive, all I wanted was for this meeting to end as quickly as possible.
It seemed like you noticed, but still tried to find new topics of conversation.
As the tea cooled off and the haze in the room dissipated, you finally stood up to leave.
Just as I closed the door and let out a sigh of relief—there went the doorbell again.
You were standing at my doorstep, inviting me to come over to Xiao Bai Tower later on.
I hadn't even had time to decline before you left down the building's exit.
I went to the kitchen and turned off the stove.
Half of the kettle had already evaporated, filling the room with a white mist.
You sat down restlessly and watched me pour tea.
"Are you still living with your grandmother and aunt?" you asked.
I told you, my grandmother had passed away, now it's just me and my aunt living together.
"She never got married," you asked.
"Yes.

The white breath you exhale, your curly hair lifted by the wind, the slight tremble of your knees under the hem of your coat—these things make me believe that you standing before me are real and not an extension of a dream I previously had.
It's no surprise that after eighteen years I don't recognize you.
You're not wearing makeup.
Your pale face is a bit bloated but at least it didn't disappoint everyone's expectations; you've grown into a beautiful woman.
Your small oval face looks gloomy though, bearing traces of having spent too much time in a big city.
You ask me if you look different than what I imagined.
Noncommittally, I merely smiled back at you.
To be honest, I had never envisioned what you would look like when grown up.

In my mind, everything concerning you has already been stored in an archive bag and sealed with lacquer wax seal —telling this might seem harsh to some people—but truthfully speaking,I didn't anticipate meeting you again.
I open my eyes.
You are standing at the door.
I don't know how long you've been standing there, perhaps long enough to have seen me laughing in my sleep, and the melancholy I feel upon waking, and how weak I am right now.
Cheng Gong, you call out my name in a low voice; your voice is so hoarse that it seems you haven't spoken for a long time.
It's about to snow the weather is heavily overcast and it's pitch black inside the house.
The water on the stove has boiled over and is gurgling noisily.
I look at you carefully for a while and convince myself that I don't recognize you.
But in this dim light, I suddenly feel that this stranger before me has some profound connection to my life—this realization sends shivers down my spine .
When trying hard to recall something , there's a swift movement of memories whirring around in my mind like shuffled cards ,then you say: "I am Li Jiaqi.
